obtained.how: article not obtained; its abstract only, as deposited with Crossref (api.crossref.org/works/10.1577/T07-256.1). Stand-in read: Irwin, B. J. 2006, PhD thesis, Cornell University, Chapter 1 'Factors affecting the success of early life stages of yellow perch in Oneida Lake, New York', from Cornell eCommons (hdl.handle.net/1813/3226)

bibliography.note: authors (Irwin, Rudstam, Jackson, VanDeValk, Forney, Fitzgerald), year, title, TAFS 138(1): 99–110 match Crossref; not checked against a title page

claims.claim: Oneida Lake, to 18 mm (egg deposition in the abstract; 8–18 mm in the project notes): larval mortality 0.042 ± 0.005 (9 yr)
claims.note: stand-in (thesis ch. 1, p. 10 = PDF p. 35): instantaneous daily mortality 0.042 ± 0.005 (N = 9 years) from the 8-mm to the 18-mm Miller-sampler survey (subset of 1968–1977, 1998, 2001), used to standardize larval density to 18 mm. In the thesis it is an 8→18-mm rate, not the egg→18-mm interval

claims.claim: Oneida Lake, 8 to 18 mm, field, 11 yr: growth 0.48 ± 0.02 (mm/d)
claims.note: stand-in (thesis p. 10 = PDF p. 35): daily growth 0.48 mm/day ± 0.02 (N = 11 years), 8-mm to 18-mm survey

claims.claim: at Oneida the winter mortality index fell as October length rose (R² = 0.382, n = 38)
claims.note: not in the abstract or the thesis chapter (the thesis credits winter mortality to Fitzgerald et al., then in press). The abstract says only that a larger end-of-year size 'should reduce subsequent mortality during the winter period'

claims.claim: Irwin et al. attribute the 1959–68 depensatory mortality to walleye consumption saturating at high perch density
claims.note: the thesis (p. 35 = PDF p. 60) says depensatory mortality was evident when walleye predation was the primary regulator (Forney 1971, 1977, 1980); saturation wording not found there

claims.claim: larval mortality was not density-dependent (R² = 0.024) but open-water growth was (R² = 0.507); larval mortality stays density-independent
claims.note: abstract: mortality 'no longer depensatory', growth 'become density dependent'. Thesis (p. 22 = PDF p. 47): mortality vs density R² = 0.023 egg–18 mm (N = 38), < 0.001 18 mm–1 Aug, 0.021 1 Aug–15 Oct; growth vs density R² = 0.506 (18 mm–1 Aug, N = 38), 0.137 (1 Aug–15 Oct, N = 43). Near but not equal to the paper's 0.024 / 0.507, so the article's figures differ from the thesis's

claims.claim: winter mortality fell with October length, so compensation now acts "through the first winter and second spring"
claims.note: the quoted phrase is not in the abstract (which speaks of 'delayed compensation that helps stabilize density at age 1') nor in the thesis chapter

claims.claim: young yellow perch live on the littoral bottom from August
claims.note: the abstract calls 1 Aug–15 Oct 'the demersal stage'; 'littoral' is not in it. The thesis samples that stage by bottom trawl at 10 standard sites and calls the fish 'primarily demersal'

notes: Recommendation: read the article itself (library login at doi:10.1577/T07-256.1) before keeping the R² values and the quoted phrase. If it stays blocked, the thesis chapter (Irwin 2006, Cornell PhD, ch. 1; eCommons hdl 1813/3226) supports, under its own citation: the 8→18-mm larval rates (mortality 0.042 ± 0.005 d⁻¹, N = 9 yr; growth 0.48 ± 0.02 mm/d, N = 11 yr; p. 10); mortality not density-dependent in any interval and growth density-dependent (R² 0.023 / 0.506; p. 22); depensatory mortality of the 1960s–early 1970s not seen in recent years (pp. 2, 35). It does not contain the winter-mortality regression (R² 0.382, n = 38) or the 'first winter and second spring' phrase.
